questions.q: What does setting a random seed such as np.random.default_rng(42) accomplish?
options: It makes the random numbers more random
It makes the random sequence repeat exactly on every run
It speeds up NumPy
It encrypts the data
questions.explain: A seed fixes the starting point of the pseudo-random sequence, so the same code produces the same numbers each time.

questions.q: You call train_test_split(df, test_size=0.3) with no random_state. What is the risk?
options: The function will raise an error
The test set will always be empty
Every row will land in the training set
The split may differ on each run, so downstream results such as model accuracy can change
questions.explain: Without random_state the shuffle is different each time, so results are not reproducible.

questions.q: What is the purpose of running pip freeze > requirements.txt and committing that file?
options: It records the exact package versions so others can recreate your environment
It uninstalls unused packages
It speeds up import statements
It backs up your data
questions.explain: requirements.txt lists installed packages and versions; pip install -r requirements.txt rebuilds that environment elsewhere.

options: CSV files cannot be read by pandas
It only works on one machine; a path built relative to the project with pathlib works wherever it is cloned
Desktop folders are read-only
pandas always ignores absolute paths
questions.explain: Hard-coded absolute paths break on any other computer. Building paths from the script's location keeps the project portable.

questions.q: What does a SHA-256 hash of your raw data file give you?
options: A compressed copy of the file
A guarantee the data is free of errors
A fingerprint that changes if the file's contents change, so you can prove which data version produced a result
A faster way to load the file
questions.explain: A hash identifies the exact bytes of a file. Store it with your results to trace them back to a specific data version.
